extracted.intended_audience: referees and authors of mathematical/computer-science journal papers (graduate students and academic authors)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for refereeing, writing, and illustrating mathematical/computer-science journal papers: how to judge publishability, what technical/style points to check, and best practices for diagrams and notation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paper recommendation categories
rubrics_metrics.description: Referees are asked to assign an overall rating by checking one of a series of boxes, ranging from (most fulsome praise) "accept", through "accept with major modifications" and "accept with minor changes" to "Reject: submit to _______."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish levels: (1) Publish essentially as is—only very simple typographical changes needed; (2) Publish after author's minor revision—referee indicates points to meet publication standards; (3) Publish only if the author makes major revisions—paper may be too long or badly written and may need re-refereeing after revision; (4) Reject—nothing salvageable. When rejecting, the referee may be asked to suggest a less prestigious journal. Use these categories to judge publishability and whether re-refereeing is appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary goals of refereeing
rubrics_metrics.description: The goals of a referee are to keep the quality of publication as high as possible and to help the author produce a better paper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write reports designed to give the author maximum benefit while not compromising on quality. Balance helpfulness with critical standards; treat refereeing as an important professional responsibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contribution to the state of the art
rubrics_metrics.description: The paper should contribute to the state of the art; if it is purely expository it should be clearly designated as such.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge whether the manuscript advances knowledge or methods in the field. For expository papers, verify that the scope and value of exposition are clear. Use this as a primary criterion for recommending publication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technical correctness
rubrics_metrics.description: All technical material must be correct (e.g., no incorrect equations); check the technical accuracy of claims, proofs, and computations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine proofs and derivations for subtle errors; referees may need to reproduce computations or write small programs to verify claims. Point out specific errors and request corrections; identify where arguments are misleading or overly subtle.

rubrics_metrics.name: English style and readability
rubrics_metrics.description: Articles should be identifiable, readable, solidly written; English style must be adequate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess clarity of prose, sentence structure, and overall readability. Recommend improvements to make exposition unambiguous and accessible. Note that poor writing can make a paper unsuitable for publication even if technically correct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adequacy of bibliography and references
rubrics_metrics.description: The bibliography should be adequate; authors should make appropriate reference to earlier work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for missing citations and suggest pertinent references. Referees often provide a 'slew of references' that can lead authors to new ideas; missing references is a common criticism, especially for authors venturing into unfamiliar fields.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timeliness of review
rubrics_metrics.description: Referees should return reviews promptly; do not postpone—e.g., a recommended turnaround is within four weeks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Remember that the review cycle is often on the critical path for publication; delay harms the process. If unable to complete a timely review, notify the editor so alternate referees can be found.

rubrics_metrics.name: Report format and confidentiality
rubrics_metrics.description: Return the manuscript to the editor (do not mark it up); submit the report in duplicate; you may write an accompanying letter to the editor and may choose whether to identify yourself in the report.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One copy of the report may go to the author (via the editor) and another to the editor. If writing a direct accompanying letter to the editor, ensure it does not constitute the referee's formal report. Be mindful about revealing your name—follow the journal's policy about anonymity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide constructive, specific feedback
rubrics_metrics.description: Referees should give concrete, actionable comments: point out typographic errors, suggest notation changes, highlight parts enjoyed, and provide references and corrections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give examples of misleading phrasing or unclear exposition and suggest precise improvements. Distinguish substantive contributions (e.g., suggested theorem improvements) from trivial edits. Helpful referees frequently provide references and constructive suggestions that improve the paper materially.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid facile generalizations (anti-pattern)
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid suggesting 'facile generalizations'—generalizations that are merely mechanical manipulations of an argument without creating new insight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When proposing extensions, ensure they add conceptual value rather than trivial parameter changes. Call out suggestions that would not increase understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seek feedback from a motivated reader
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors should solicit feedback from motivated readers (referees value this); referees likewise provide valuable motivated-reader feedback.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage authors to get early feedback and to use referees' comments to improve presentations and discover relevant literature. Referees are part of a cooperative system where mutual improvement is expected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anonymity and identity considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: The identities of referees are usually hidden from authors; some journals hide authors' identities from referees; author names can strongly affect readers' reactions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware of the journal's anonymity policy. Authors sometimes use pseudonyms or submit to journals with different refereeing rigor; consider how identity or lack thereof might bias evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Title clarity and ambiguity avoidance
rubrics_metrics.description: Titles must be unambiguous and clearly indicate the subject (avoid titles that can be read in multiple ways).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a title could be misread (e.g., 'Optimal Font Caching' meaning either 'caching of optimal fonts' or 'optimal caching'), suggest a clearer title. Small changes can resolve ambiguity and better set reader expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diagrams: size and level of detail
rubrics_metrics.description: Diagrams are useful if kept small; details may be included for those who want them but should not hinder readers who don't need the detail.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use diagrams to help readers grasp algorithms or structures; avoid oversized or overly detailed figures that confuse rather than clarify. If detailed figures are necessary, design them so readers can ignore minutiae if desired.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of color and illustrations
rubrics_metrics.description: Color can be effective in talks but usually not in papers; illustrations are indispensable in many cases but greatly increase preparation workload.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be conservative about color in print papers; evaluate whether an illustration adds clarity sufficient to justify the extra production effort (the author quips that work is roughly proportional to the cube of the number of illustrations). Place explanatory text opposite the diagrams they refer to and be mindful of printing issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use real data/examples rather than 'cooked' samples
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer 'real' data or canonical examples (e.g., a paragraph from Grimm's Fairy Tales) to artificially cooked sample data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Real data demonstrates practical behavior and can reveal issues that contrived examples miss. Warn against examples designed solely to fit an exposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diagrams and alternative forms (nested diagrams, ATNs, etc.)
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider alternative diagram forms (nested diagrams, ATNs) to replace traditional trees or to illustrate parsing and state transitions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose the diagram style that best conveys the concept (e.g., nested boxes for hierarchical structure, augmented transition networks for parsing). Use diagrams adapted from established sources (Tufte, Winograd) when helpful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tables and listings for asynchronous processes
rubrics_metrics.description: For some phenomena (e.g., asynchronous processes), a listing of events or tables may convey essential features more clearly than typical graphics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose the representation (table, listing, diagram) that most clearly conveys the behavior; sometimes a numerical table reveals patterns that graphs obscure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof exposition: factorization and orientation
rubrics_metrics.description: Factor proofs into subgoals, provide orientation (e.g., 'this is essentially a diagonalization technique'), and aim to minimize what readers must keep in mind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Break proofs into clear components with simple interfaces and state the overall strategy. Such factoring reduces cognitive load and makes proofs easier to follow; graders/readers find oriented, factored proofs easier to understand.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimize complicated notation (subscripts/superscripts)
rubrics_metrics.description: Aim for notation that needs no double subscripts or subscripted superscripts; minimize subscripts and superscripts to improve clarity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recast proofs or constructions to avoid nested indices. Use plain words where notation would obfuscate. Homework assignment guidance: simplify Gillman's version further so no subscripted subscripts/superscripts remain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be explicit about deliberate presentation choices (printer behavior)
rubrics_metrics.description: When including deliberate visual examples (e.g., deliberately 'ugly' typesetting), inform printers/editors so they don't 'correct' them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a figure or typesetting choice is intentionally illustrating a point, note this in communications to printers or editors to prevent unintended 'corrections'.
